elements.content:
• What is HTML and why it matters

• Course objectives

• Structure of today’s lesson

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Ms. Clara Finch, and today we’re kicking off our journey into HTML. Let’s start by understanding what HTML is and why it matters.
First, HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It’s the backbone of every web page, letting us structure content like headings, paragraphs, images, and links.
Our course objectives are simple: by the end of this session you’ll be able to write basic HTML tags, create a simple webpage, and understand how browsers interpret your code.
Finally, let’s look at today’s lesson structure: we’ll cover core tags, practice building a page together, and finish with a quick hands‑on challenge.
That’s our roadmap for the next hour—feel free to ask questions at any time, and Alex will be here to help you try things out as we go.

elements.content: Basic HTML Document Structure

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s explore the basic structure every HTML page needs. This is the foundation that lets browsers understand and display our web content.
First, the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration. Think of it as a quick note to the browser saying, “Hey, this is an HTML5 document,” so it knows how to interpret everything that follows.

Next, the three core tags: <html>, <head>, and <body>. The <html> tag wraps the whole page, <head> holds metadata like the title and links to stylesheets, and <body> contains everything the user actually sees.
Inside the <head> section, we place the <title> tag. This is what appears on the browser tab and helps identify the page in search results.

Here’s a simple, complete example combining all these pieces. Notice how the doctype comes first, then the <html> wrapper, followed by <head> with the title, and finally the <body> where we could add headings, paragraphs, and images.

To recap, every HTML page starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, then the <html> element containing a <head> for metadata – including the <title> – and a <body> for visible content. Mastering this skeleton sets you up for all the exciting web building ahead.

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Ms. Clara Finch. Today we'll explore how to structure our web pages with headings and paragraphs.
First, look at the slide title: **Headings and Paragraphs**. This tells us the two core building blocks we'll cover.
Now, notice the bullet points. The first point mentions the heading tags <h1> through <h6>. These tags create a clear hierarchy, just like chapters and sub‑chapters in a book.

The second bullet reminds us to use the

tag for paragraphs. Think of

as a separate block of text, similar to a paragraph in a magazine article.
Finally, the third point highlights best practices for semantic hierarchy—using headings in order without skipping levels, so screen readers and search engines can understand the structure.
To sum up, headings organize your content into sections, and paragraphs fill those sections with readable text. We'll soon practice by building a simple page together.

elements.content:
• Create hyperlinks: <a href="URL">link text</a>

• Embed images: <img src="URL" alt="description">

• Use meaningful alt text for accessibility

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into our next topic: Links and Images. These two elements let you navigate between pages and add visual interest to your site.
First, creating a hyperlink is as simple as wrapping the text you want clickable inside an tag with an href attribute. For example, Visit Example makes the words “Visit Example” a link.
Notice the structure: the opening , the link text, and the closing . The URL can point to another page, a file, or even an email address.
Next, to embed an image we use the tag with a src attribute that tells the browser where the picture lives, and an alt attribute that describes the image for accessibility.
A meaningful alt text, like alt="smiling student holding a laptop", helps screen‑readers and improves SEO, so always write a short, descriptive phrase.
To recap, we just covered how to build hyperlinks with and how to insert images using while remembering the importance of good alt text. Any quick questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• <ol> for numbered lists

• <ul> for bullet lists

• <li> for each list item

• Nesting lists for complex outlines

actions.text: All right, everyone, let's dive into lists in HTML. We'll see how to create ordered and unordered lists to organize content on a page.

First, the <ol> tag creates a numbered list, perfect for steps or rankings. Next, the <ul> tag gives you a bullet list for items that don't need a specific order. Each individual item, whether in an ordered or unordered list, is wrapped in an <li> tag. And finally, you can nest lists inside one another to build more complex outlines, like a list of topics with sub‑topics beneath each.

Remember, the structure is simple: a list container (<ol> or <ul>) holds one or more <li> elements, and you can place another <ol> or <ul> inside an <li> to create nesting. That's all for lists—feel free to try coding a few examples now!

elements.content:
• Core tags: <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>

• Adding headers and rows

• Simple styling tips

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Ms. Clara Finch, and today we're diving into HTML tables—your tool for displaying data in rows and columns.
First, let's look at the core tags: <table> creates the table container, <tr> defines a table row, <th> marks a header cell, and <td> holds regular data cells.
To add headers, place <th> elements inside a <tr> at the top of the table. Each subsequent <tr> will contain <td> cells for the data rows.
A quick styling tip: you can add a simple border with the CSS rule table, th, td { border: 1px solid #ccc; } to make the grid visible.
That covers the basics—core tags, how to structure headers and rows, and a simple style to get you started. Any questions before we move on to our hands‑on practice?

elements.content:
• Form container: <form>

• Input elements: <input>, <textarea>, <button>

• Use <label> for accessibility

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into the basics of HTML forms. This slide is titled **Forms Basics**, and we'll explore how to collect user input on a webpage.
First, every form starts with a **form container** using the `<form>` tag. Think of it like a bowl that holds all the ingredients you want to gather from a user.
Inside the form, we place **input elements** such as `<input>` for single‑line fields, `<textarea>` for multi‑line text, and `<button>` to submit the data.
Finally, pairing each input with a `<label>` improves accessibility. The label describes the purpose of the field and lets screen readers convey the right information.
That's the core of building a simple form: a container, the input fields, and accessible labels. Any questions before we move on to a quick hands‑on example?

elements.content: Purpose of semantic tags for structure & accessibility

• Sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves SEO and aids screen readers

• Replace generic <div> when content has a specific meaning

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into Semantic HTML and see how it helps us give meaning to our web pages.
First, we have the sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. Each of these tells browsers and assistive tools what kind of content lives inside.
Using these tags improves SEO because search engines can more easily understand the page structure, and it makes screens readers navigate the page more intuitively.

When you see a generic <div> that’s just grouping content, ask yourself: does this block represent a header, navigation, an article, or the main content? If so, replace the <div> with the appropriate semantic tag.
That’s the big picture—clear structure, better accessibility, and stronger search performance. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Consistent indentation for readability

• Structured heading hierarchy (h1‑h6)

• Descriptive alt text for images

• Use semantic elements (section, article, nav)

actions.text: Now let's talk about Good Coding Practices for HTML. Keeping our markup clean makes it easier to read, maintain, and collaborate on.

First, consistent indentation improves readability – think of it like neat paragraphs in a book. Next, use meaningful heading hierarchy so screen readers and search engines understand the structure. Then, always add descriptive alt text to images so everyone knows what they represent. Finally, rely on semantic elements like <header>, <nav>, and <section> instead of generic <div>s for clearer meaning.
By following these simple guidelines, your HTML will stay organized and accessible, making future updates a breeze.
